question: In Java, which of the following is a strict requirement for a subclass method to successfully override an instance method defined in its superclass?

options.text: The subclass method must have the exact same method name and parameter list as the superclass method.
The subclass method must be declared with a more restrictive access modifier than the superclass method.
The subclass method must include the @Override annotation, or the compiler will treat it as an unrelated method.
The subclass method can have a completely different parameter list as long as its return type is identical.

explanation: Method overriding requires the subclass method to have the exact same signature (name and parameter types) as the superclass method. Option B is incorrect because visibility cannot be reduced. Option C is wrong because @Override is optional compiler metadata. Option D describes overloading, not overriding.

question: What happens if a subclass attempts to declare a method with the exact same signature as a final instance method in its superclass?

options.text: The subclass method successfully overrides the superclass method at runtime.
A compile-time error occurs because final methods cannot be overridden.
The subclass method overloads the final method, making both accessible depending on arguments.
The code compiles successfully but throws an UnsupportedOperationException when executed.

explanation: Marking an instance method as final explicitly prohibits subclasses from overriding it; any attempt to do so produces a compilation error. Option A reflects the false belief that final methods can still be overridden. Option C is wrong because identical signatures cannot overload.

explanation: Because start() is an overridden instance method, dynamic method dispatch invokes the implementation corresponding to the actual runtime object (Car), printing 'Car '. Option 'Vehicle ' falsely assumes reference type determines instance method dispatch.

Runtime error because SuperClass cannot hold an instance of SubClass.
Compile-time error because execute must return an int.
Compile-time error because SubClass cannot assign weaker access privileges (protected) than SuperClass (public).

explanation: An overriding method cannot reduce the visibility of the method it overrides. In SuperClass, execute() is public; in SubClass, declaring it protected reduces visibility, causing a compilation error. Option A assumes access privileges can be reduced.

Super Sub

explanation: Static methods are hidden, not overridden. Calls to static methods are bound at compile time based on the reference type (SuperType), so 'Super ' is printed. Option 'Sub ' assumes static methods participate in runtime polymorphism.

options.text: Dog must use the @Override annotation to compile.
Dog defines makeSound() with an incompatible return type (int instead of void) for overriding.
Subclasses are not allowed to override methods that have no parameters.
Animal cannot be instantiated because its method has a body.

explanation: When overriding a method with the same parameter signature, the return type must be identical or covariant. Changing void to int is not a valid override and causes a compile-time clash. Option C confuses overloading with overriding.

explanation: FastCalculator defines compute(double, int), which overloads rather than overrides compute(int, double). Since reference 'c' is of type Calculator, calling compute(4, 2.0) resolves to Calculator's method, returning 4 + 2.0 = 6.0. Option '8.0' mistakenly treats parameter reordering as an override.

question: Which statement correctly describes the role of the @Override annotation on a Java method?

options.text: It changes the dispatch mechanism of the method from static to dynamic.
It is mandatory; the JVM will ignore subclass overrides at runtime without it.
It enables the method to override final methods defined in parent classes.
It instructs the compiler to verify that the method actually overrides a declaration in a supertype.

explanation: The @Override annotation is a compile-time check ensuring the annotated method properly overrides a method in a superclass or interface. If no matching supertype method exists, compilation fails. Option B is wrong because overrides work even without the annotation.

options.text: Compile-time error because overriding methods must have the identical return type, not a subtype.
ClassCastException at runtime when assigning Derived to Base.

explanation: Java supports covariant return types: an overriding method can return a subtype (Integer) of the superclass method's return type (Number). At runtime, dynamic dispatch invokes Derived.getValue(), printing 20. Option C fails to recognize covariant return types.

options.text: Compile-time error because secret cannot be declared public in Child.
Compile-time error because secret() in Parent is private, so Child does not override it and @Override is invalid.
Compile-time error because static method secret() cannot be called on instance c.
No compile error; code runs and prints "Child secret".

explanation: Private methods in a superclass are not visible to subclasses and cannot be overridden. In Child, secret() is an independent new method, causing the @Override annotation to fail compilation. Option A falsely claims expanding visibility is illegal.

options.text: Beta-String
Compilation error because Beta does not override test(Object).
Alpha-Object
Beta-String Alpha-Object

explanation: Beta.test(String) overloads, rather than overrides, Alpha.test(Object). The variable 'a' has declared type Alpha, which only knows test(Object). Therefore, compile-time signature resolution chooses test(Object), and dynamic dispatch calls Alpha's implementation, printing 'Alpha-Object '. Option 'Beta-String ' confuses overloading with overriding.

question: Suppose class A declares protected Number calculate(int n). Which of the following signatures in a subclass B extends A is a legal override in Java?

options.text: public Double calculate(long n)
private Integer calculate(int n)
protected Object calculate(int n)
public Integer calculate(int n)

explanation: A valid override must have the identical parameter list (int n), can widen access (protected to public), and can use a covariant return type (Integer is a subtype of Number). Option A changes parameter type (overload). Option B reduces visibility. Option C widens return type to Object, which is illegal.
